title: 7.1 Journaling Like a Risk Manager
summary: Many beginners think a journal is just a place to write:
bodyHtml:
7.1 Journaling Like a Risk Manager

Why This Matters

Many beginners think a journal is just a place to write:

won money today

or

bad day, need to do better

That is not enough.

A useful trading journal is not mainly about emotion. It is about evidence.

A risk manager wants records that answer simple questions:

  • What was the plan?
  • What actually happened?
  • Where did the trade follow the rules?
  • Where did the trader break the rules?

If your journal cannot answer those questions, it cannot help you improve.

What You Should Understand After This Lesson

By the end of this lesson, you should be able to:

  • explain why a journal should record process, not just profit or loss;
  • identify the minimum fields needed for a useful journal entry;
  • use the journal to compare the planned trade with the real trade.

Think of a Journal as a Verification Tool

Investor.gov tells investors to review account statements and trade confirmations carefully so they can verify what happened in the account.

Your personal trading journal should do something similar for your own process.

It should help you verify:

  • the idea you wanted to trade;
  • the risk you meant to take;
  • the risk you actually took;
  • the behavior you showed during the trade.

That is why a journal is closer to a lab notebook than a diary.

The Minimum Useful Journal Entry

Field What to record Why it matters
Setup Market, wrapper, direction, and basic trade idea Shows what you were trying to do
Risk plan Entry, stop, target, size, and planned money risk Shows whether the math was clear before entry
Execution Actual entry, actual exit, and any changes made during the trade Shows whether you followed the plan
Context Session, event risk, market family, or unusual conditions Helps explain timing and volatility
Behavior Emotional state or behavior trigger Helps identify revenge trading, hesitation, or boredom trading
Lesson One short note on what to repeat or fix next time Turns the entry into an improvement tool

(Table alt-text: A six-row table listing the minimum useful parts of a trade journal and why each part matters.)

Screenshots Help Your Memory

Words are helpful, but pictures can reveal details that memory hides.

If possible, save:

  • one chart image near entry;
  • one chart image near exit.

Screenshots help you review:

  • whether the setup actually matched your written idea;
  • whether the stop was placed where you said it would be;
  • whether you exited because of the plan or because of emotion.

The image does not replace the note. It supports the note.

One Multi-Market Example

Imagine your journal for one week includes:

  • EUR/USD: long pullback, planned risk USD 50, respected the stop;
  • S&P 500 index product: long breakout, planned risk USD 60, entered five minutes before a major event;
  • Gold: long trend trade, took profit too early from fear;
  • Brent crude: long setup, widened the stop and doubled the loss.

If the journal only records money, the week looks like random good and bad luck.

If the journal records:

  • planned risk versus actual risk;
  • market family and wrapper;
  • event context;
  • behavior notes;

then the real pattern becomes visible.

Maybe the biggest issue was not chart reading at all. Maybe it was:

  • poor timing in the index trade;
  • fear in the gold trade;
  • rule-breaking in the Brent trade.

That is the whole point of journaling.

Common Beginner Mistakes

Mistake 1: Recording Only Profit or Loss

Money tells you the outcome. It does not tell you the quality of the process.

Mistake 2: Journaling Only the Good Trades

Your most valuable entries are often the trades where discipline broke down.

Mistake 3: Writing Vague Notes

bad trade is not useful. entered during news and ignored my risk limit is useful.

Mistake 4: Skipping the Review Note

If you do not name the lesson, you are less likely to change the behavior.
